observations.why: A starts with the member’s task and brings matching irons into view. B starts with a pickup window and carries that choice into the iron request.

A filters by task to show suitable tools. B filters by pickup window before the request, but the facts give current stock and collection hours without establishing which tools are available at each window.
A lets members request an iron directly from inventory. B starts with the job and reveals the iron request beside the task choices on desktop or directly under Solder on a phone.
A starts with item status and lets members request from an available row. B starts with the attempted task and shows matching tools, availability, and pickup information below the prompt.
A shows suitable items and their eligibility before the member requests one. B starts with inventory and uses the request itself to open the inline suitability, induction, and pickup confirmation.
A opens with the iron and a direct request action. B asks what the member wants to do, then shows the matching tool and status beneath the selected task.

A leads with the harvest note and confirms under the time selector. B leads with the marked map, showing the open rows and gravel shop route in relation to the muddy north rows, and confirms beneath the map.

A gives visitors the access update in prose and opens the time picker directly. B starts with the map and asks visitors to choose a visit type first. Picking reveals times, while shop-only highlights the gravel path.

A opens with booking and walk-in panels, with row conditions on the map below. B puts access conditions first and asks visitors to choose picking or shopping before showing times or confirming walk-in access.
A opens the slot picker from the picking option and confirms there. B makes either open row on the map an entry point to Saturday times beneath the map, with the shop route labeled separately.
A leads with visit options and opens times beneath the booking button. B shows the gravel bypass in relation to the rows before visitors act, and its shop control highlights that route on the map.

Both open and confirm reservations beneath the visit options. A leads with the harvest note and basket photo. B places the labeled map beside the options on desktop and directly below them on phones, making the gravel bypass visible in relation to the rows.
A starts with all three dates and expands evidence beneath the selected card. B starts with the 2025 recording and transcript, then replaces the evidence pane when visitors choose an older record.

A lets visitors choose by year and see the 1978 scan beside or below the ferry photo. B exposes the abutment and steps before their dates, so visitors choose a known location and discover its dated record.

A presents the full timeline before visitors choose a record. B starts with two known locations and a ferry-era section, so visitors can find media by landmark while reading the ferry photo in the context of the changed bend.

A starts with the ferry photo and swaps records in a year-indexed viewer. B opens with the scan and audio together, then adds the ferry photo beneath both while keeping playback and transcript controls available.

A starts with the ferry photo and uses a dated rail to reveal evidence in a detail panel. B presents all three records as source rows, with playback, progress, and transcript available within the recording’s own row.

A keeps the ferry photo and high-water scan visible together for image comparison. B keeps the recording and transcript as the reference, then brings in either historical image alongside or below the recording.

A starts with access and reveals courtyard and bell directions on tap. B establishes that visitors can just arrive, then makes choosing a time for optional help the first interaction and displays it in the request summary.

A puts entrance choice first and expands bell instructions under the courtyard route. B puts hours and quiet hour first on phones, then shows the chosen time beside the volunteer request. Both support walk-in access.

A starts with an entrance selector and displays the chosen route below it. B puts the entry photo first on phones and opens a time picker for courtyard help, with the chosen time shown in a pending summary.

A expands courtyard directions and the optional request together beside or below the photo. Its form can include the 30-minute notice. B makes the form directly available and keeps the chosen time visible after sending.

A puts route text above the photo on phones and offers a directly available time field. B puts the photo first for recognition and expands the courtyard directions and volunteer form together beneath it.

A uses the photo for recognition and reveals step-free directions first. The lower-priority volunteer form can show the chosen time and notice. B starts with time selection and displays the result above the optional courtyard request.
A starts with production dates and shows conflicts on the rail. B starts by collecting fit and restriction evidence in a comparison panel, where borrowers then check dates and request pieces.

A groups facts and eligibility by garment card. B aligns the same fields across garments for direct comparison. A leaves it unclear whether the alteration status displaces Request. B leaves it unclear when an unavailable appointment would block a loan.

Both show fit and restriction evidence beside garment photos, then use production dates to reveal request actions or blockers on each piece. The diary and photo emphasis leave the decision order and result placement the same.
A starts with dates and updates eligibility on each card. B starts with large detail photographs and puts fit comparison in a tray before asking for dates and showing request outcomes there.

A starts with dates and reports eligibility on each card. B starts by selecting a piece on a timeline and reveals evidence and dependencies below. B makes an alteration appointment a prerequisite without a stated loan rule supporting it.
A uses dates to build a shortlist with outcomes on the garment cards. B starts with fit evidence and lets borrowers pin pieces in a tray before checking dates and intended use there.

A updates an ordered itinerary after route selection. B makes the bridge a pass-through stage and replaces that stage with the next reachable stop. It is unclear how someone starting at the square reaches the route choices on a phone.

A starts with direct versus step-free access. B starts with departure time and uses it to determine which stops remain feasible. The choir cutoff is known, but departure time alone cannot establish whether walkers will reach it in time.
Both start with the same crossing choice and update a next-stop card. B moves the controls to the bottom and gives the photo more space, with the same route decision and next-stop information.

B adds a Start tap and surfaces the bell preview earlier. Both still require the same route choice to reveal the next reachable stop. Both promise arrival times, which the supplied facts do not establish.

A starts route planning at the square and explicitly leaves the next stop’s timing unlisted. B lets walkers choose a route from the bridge and shows the choir’s cutoff alongside the onward directions.

A starts with the crossing choice. B starts with whether to include the choir and opens the step-free route when selected. The facts do not tie choir access to that crossing, and the phone sketch leaves it unclear whether walkers can change routes.
